This paper introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. To facilitate adoption, we have made the R-package implementing TV-PARX available at https://github.com/CountModels/CountAutoModels/. Keywords: Count time series; Nonlinear models; Score-driven models; Structural breaks; TV-PARX; Italy COVID-19; US corporate defaults. JEL classification: C01; C22.
Although the concept of employing stellar photometry to monitor the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the CRAB high-z transient survey and recent pilot observations from a portable 15 cm telescope, we present the most precise calibration-by-product VAOD measurements to date. When calibrated against sunphotometer readings, our method achieves a precision of 0.007 VAOD. By utilizing extensive VAOD datasets to characterize calibration systematics, we demonstrate that combining stellar photometry with iridescence imaging can yield even greater precision. Furthermore, we outline a practical strategy for deploying this approach in the field as a calibrated-by-product service. This technique offers a rapid, real-time, and potentially cost-effective solution for calibrating sunphotometers, provided the underlying photometric method is sufficiently precise. As an independent measurement technique reliant on the atmosphere rather than complex instruments, it also functions effectively as a cross-check for other methods, such as radiometric diffuser cards, without requiring direct visual observation of the sun. To maximize the utility of VAOD data derived from stellar photometry, we recommend adopting a few standard practices. These include utilizing narrow-band photometry around the V filter center, employing atmosphere-transparent imaging filters for iridescence, and employing precise CCD or CMOS sensors with linear responses, all while meticulously documenting specific observational conditions.
This study evaluates and compares numerous numerical techniques for addressing stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics, which rely on combinations of deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. In general systems, an optimal method is identified that exhibits significantly lower bias than alternatives. Simulations of the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) demonstrate that this approach achieves higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency, supports larger timesteps, and maintains the conformational exploration rate. The proposed scheme represents a uniformly superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering practical timestep increases of over 25% in vacuum and reducing errors in configurational averages by more than a factor of ten in solvated simulations at large timesteps. It is implemented in GROMOS, AMBER, and CHARMM force fields, rendering it broadly applicable. The theoretical framework and findings regarding sampling accuracy and exploration rate may also prove useful for other molecular dynamics methods facing limitations at large timesteps, such as coarse-grained models. As an example application, the study examines the feasibility of tensor network molecular dynamics for complex systems like protein-ligand interactions.
Current automatic image description models are typically trained and assessed using crowdsourced human-generated captions, with system performance measured by similarity metrics such as BLEU, Meteor, and CIDER. Consequently, the reliability of both the systems and their evaluation hinges on the quality of these reference descriptions. As demonstrated in Section 2, existing image description datasets lack sufficient quality. I contend that more detailed guidelines are necessary, ones that balance the specific requirements of visually impaired users with the practical feasibility of generating appropriate descriptions. While high-quality data would allow for reference-based evaluation, we should also explore alternative assessment methods. These could involve comparing systems on their ability to prioritize information in unknown images against human raters, or analyzing the feasibility of validating visual claims made in generated descriptions through human feedback. Ultimately, the success of automatic image description systems will ultimately depend on their end-users: visually impaired individuals. Therefore, direct evaluation by this community regarding the utility of such systems for their personal lives is essential. I hope this perspective encourages the collection of higher-quality data and the development of better evaluation frameworks. Ultimately, visually impaired users will determine whether these systems meet their needs.

Additional findings explore the geometric characteristics of this bound and its relationship to entropy, as well as the asymptotic behavior of operator complexity across short, long, and intermediate times.

This section examines predictions from the bilepton model, an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics comprises bileptons and three heavy quarks, ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. While QCD will bind these heavy quarks with light quarks and among themselves to create baryons and mesons, these composite particles will remain undetectable at the LHC but could be observed at a hypothetical 100 TeV proton-proton collider, unlike the bileptons. Detecting both the bileptons and these quark-bound states would provide compelling evidence for this model and serve as strong indicators for a larger unifying gauge group, $SU(3) \times SU(3) \times U(1)$, emerging from Grand Unified Theory. A minimal supersymmetric variant of this framework is also detailed. Given that QCD will form baryons and mesons from the three new heavy quarks—analogue to how charm and strange quarks create $D$ and $S$ baryons and mesons—this paper concentrates on the properties of these ${{\cal T}}$-baryons and bibeptons. Additionally, this work highlights the challenges in detecting bibeptons at both the LHC and a 100 TeV collider. Finally, it examines how these bibeptons could influence ultra-high-energy cosmic ray bibepton cross-sections and interactions, potentially resolving the "missing energy" anomaly reported by the ALEX experiment when comparing proton-atmosphere cross-sections to those at the LHC.
This paper introduces IDET systems grounded in SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM, serving as the counterparts to our optimal wideband waveforming approach detailed in [1]. We formulate optimization problems aimed at maximizing both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Leveraging a fixed-point based alternating algorithm, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput solutions for both SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM configurations. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the fair-throughput benefit observed in wideband systems extends equally to OFDM systems. Furthermore, simulations compare the fair-throughput and sum-throughput performance of the ideal systems described in [1] alongside our SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM solutions. Finally, a real-time implementation of the system is presented and tested via a wireless connection between a PC and a smartphone.
Fitting Parton Distribution Functions (PDFs) demands a unified framework that integrates extensive datasets from both theoretical predictions and experimental data. While data integration primarily involves standardizing formats, incorporating theoretical predictions is more complex due to the involvement of multiple components. Various independent groups develop distinct providers for different processes, utilizing diverse input parameters (runcards) and output structures (interpolation grids). Furthermore, because processes are measured across different scales, the PDF candidate requires DGLAP evolution, either calculated dynamically or precomputed into grids. Our goal is to automate all these steps within a single framework, making it a valuable resource for any PDF fitting group and potentially for broader phenomenological investigations. To achieve this, we have developed a Python library called Sambar ($\text{http://inspirehep.net/show-abstract?absId=1604.06829$}$), which serves as the successor to Retina and partially builds upon Weasel. This presentation will outline the necessary ingredients for a framework like Sambar and demonstrate its application through specific examples.
This research conducts a linear analysis of a turbulent methane-air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Ultimately, the a priori analysis confirmed that the linearized RANS-EBU model accurately represents LES reaction rate fluctuations, whereas the linearized LES-EBU model introduces spurious modes associated with acoustic oscillations. This occurs because LES attempts to resolve reaction rate oscillations directly, which conflicts with its assumption that turbulent and acoustic eddies are separable. Consequently, the a priori approach validated here offers a cost-effective method for testing combustion models against LES, serving as an alternative to direct linearization within LES or DNS frameworks. Additionally, this method could prove valuable for optimizing control strategies in actively controlled jets by selecting appropriate combustion models. Regarding the linearized RANS-EBU model's accuracy, its performance relies heavily on the eddy damping factor ($\chi$) in the EBU model, which links turbulent and acoustic eddies. Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a classical, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, the constitutive relation is optimized to ensure the resulting field equations remain linear with respect to the higher-derivative nonlocal terms; under these conditions, a new effective potential is also investigated.

The detection of certain variable X-ray sources in the Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. Finally, we argue that future searches for transient LMXBs are more likely to succeed by targeting systems with infrequent outbursts, perhaps by examining those that display the longest variable timescales. To address this, we introduce a new sample of centre-Galaxy variable sources discovered by searching for transients in the light curves of images from the Deep Field Survey.
Bipartite graphs represent the connections between two separate sets of entities. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, we provide an explicit formula for this minimum $k$ under the condition that the graph admits a "almost planar" structure, differing from a planar configuration by a small distance. Finally, we outline how these findings can be applied to automate the construction of planar visualizations by prioritizing the smallest number of split vertices. These objectives are relevant to information visualization, particularly for large-scale datasets, where such diagrams help identify patterns, clusters, and anomalies within the underlying data. As expected, our result regarding the structure of nearly planar bipartite graphs resembles the classic characterization of planar graphs by Euler. By extending this approach to higher dimensions, one could potentially generalize Euler's formula for multiway relationships (see, e.g., ).
Performance degradation techniques serve as a crucial complement to side-channel attacks. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel method that integrates prior strategies with simultaneous multithreading (SMT) architectures. Beyond this new technique, we identify a previously unrecognized source of slowdown by analyzing cache eviction as a root cause. The resulting performance degradation is substantially greater than previous methods, thereby enhancing the time granularity available for Flush+Reload attacks. We evaluated HyperDegrade across various Intel microarchitectures, achieving significant slowdowns that, in specific microbenchmark scenarios, represent a three-order-of-magnitude improvement over state-of-the-art solutions. To assess the effectiveness of performance degradation in amplifying side channels, we introduced and validated specific leakage metrics. Our findings indicate that HyperDegrade improves time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, we conducted a fair comparison of three performance degradation strategies when paired with Flush+Reload from an attacker's viewpoint. We also devised an attack targeting an underutilized vulnerability in OpenSSL, where HyperDegrade demonstrated superior performance by reducing the number of required Flush+Reload traces needed for success by a factor of three. In terms of cryptographic contributions, we revisited the recently proposed Raccoon attack on TLS-DH key exchanges, extending its application to other protocols. Leveraging HyperDegrade, we constructed an end-to-end attack proving that Raccoon-like exploits can succeed with real data, addressing a gap left by earlier research. Finally, we constructed a similar attack illustrating how Hyperscan vulnerabilities can be exploited in real-world scenarios, which was previously considered impossible. All source codes, microbenchmarks, real-world demonstrations, and the enhanced OpenSSL and Hyperscan protocols are accessible at https://github.com/will-ca/perf_degrade.
An unknotting operation represents a local modification applied to knot diagrams. It is possible to convert any knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram through a combination of unknotting operations and Reidemeister moves. These operations hold substantial significance in knot theory, particularly for analyzing knot complexity and invariants. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in fields such as biology, chemistry, and physics, where they help investigate the complex entanglements found in strings, organic molecules, and DNA. This paper introduces a novel unknotting operation known as the diagonal move, applicable to both classical and welded knots. We demonstrate that the crossing change, Delta-move, Sharp-move, Gamma-move, n-gon move, pass move, and 4-move can all be achieved via sequences of diagonal moves. Additionally, we define a distance metric based on the diagonal move and examine its characteristics. Finally, we calculate the diagonal distance for specific examples, illustrating the method's utility in assessing entanglement levels among classical and welded knots. The findings presented here extend previous research on unknotting operations and the associated distance metrics. All current studies on classical and welded knot distances and invariants are accessible at https://georgeburdick.github.io/WeldedKnots/. These resources may be adapted to classify classical knots using the diagonal move distance. Moreover, the diagonal move could serve as a valuable tool in biology, chemistry, and physics for studying the entanglement of DNA and organic molecules. Regarding the classification of classical and welded knots, the diagonal move distance could potentially function as an additional invariant to help distinguish between different classical and welded knot types.
Coordination serves as a vital capability in multi-agent systems, enabling the completion of objectives that single agents cannot achieve alone. This study examines how a team of strategic agents selects among multiple tasks within a stochastic framework, specifically focusing on two tasks with randomly distributed and partially observable difficulties. We demonstrate that when prior distributions regarding task difficulty are diffuse, a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, intuitive linear structure emerges. Conversely, we find that if the prior distribution is not diffuse, an agent's best response to an affine strategy profile may become nonlinear. Furthermore, we present an algorithm capable of efficiently calculating a data-driven Nash equilibrium restricted to the class of affine policies. Through numerical examples, we compare the performance of different policy classes, confirming that the Nash equilibrium yields superior performance compared to any alternative policy profile. Additionally, we develop an best-response-based algorithm designed to maximize the expected utility of a specific task type; however, we also illustrate that such an algorithm is not guaranteed to converge. Finally, we derive an explicit upper bound for the time required to execute N copies of the task type with the highest expected utility. The results from our analysis, numerical simulations, and experiments suggest that, under a uniform prior distribution for task difficulty, this best-response algorithm would select the correct task type with near-certainty, provided that N is sufficiently small and the range of possible utility realizations is sufficiently narrow. Our work utilizes Markov decision processes (MDPs) modified with rank-1 stochastic observations, and we detail the specific assumptions made concerning the probability distributions of tasks and their difficulties.
This paper demonstrates the embedding of regularly acting groups and diagonal groups into wreath products under their product action by utilizing Cartesian Decomposition. Additionally, the authors derive the explicit formula for this explicit construction. Furthermore, they present explicit formulations for the Cartesian Product and its inverse. The significance of this work lies in the fact that embedding acting groups into wreath products under their product action constitutes a crucial step toward determining the general product action, including its explicit structure. Finally, two illustrative examples are provided to demonstrate the proposed construction method. The explicit nature of this approach also facilitates the computation of product actions for groups that act regularly. To facilitate these calculations, we integrated our construction with the computer algebra system GAP.
The high-frequency sensitivity of gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by quantum shot noise and ultimately by optical losses within the signal-recycling cavity. This limitation represents a primary barrier to detecting gravitational waves from binary neutron star mergers in both current and future detectors, as it remains independent of arm length and the level of injected squeezing. In this study, we propose a sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, derived from a Michelson interferometer by optically linking the end mirrors to form an additional cavity. This configuration creates a triply-coupled cavity system capable of surpassing the loss-induced high-frequency limit inherent to signal-recycled Michelson interferometers. Using parameters comparable to advanced LIGO+, a sloshing-Sagnac design could achieve sevenfold improved sensitivity at 2.5 kHz, or a fourfold increase in signal-to-noise ratio for typical post-merger binary neutron star waveforms. As an evolution of the Michelson architecture, the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer offers a viable topology for upgrading current detectors and for future-generation observatories.
Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems represent a promising solution for delivering ultra-high data rates in environments with high user density. Because the physical dimensions of XL-MIMO arrays are comparable to the distances separating them from user equipments (UEs), the system experiences spatial non-stationarities and distinct visibility regions (VRs). These factors, combined with high UE density and limited pilot resources, make the design of random access (RA) protocols and scheduling algorithms particularly difficult. This paper introduces a joint RA and scheduling approach called the non-overlapping VR XL-MIMO (NOVR-XL) protocol. This method leverages the unique VRs of individual UEs to enhance RA performance and prioritizes scheduling UEs with non-overlapping VRs within the same payload data pilot resource. Simulation results demonstrate that this proposed scheme yields substantial improvements in sum rate compared to conventional RA methods, while also lowering access latency and overall connectivity performance. Furthermore, the NOVR-XL method exhibits remarkable scalability; as the number of antennas grows, its sum rate approaches that of the perfect VR system (PVR-XL), ultimately achieving nearly identical performance under specific conditions. To facilitate these findings, we also develop a closed-form expression for the signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) within the VR of a target UE.
Although neural language models have largely replaced traditional $N$-gram models due to superior performance, our findings suggest that $N$-grams still yield satisfactory results in many scenarios, effectively capturing significant linguistic knowledge at a low computational cost. Leveraging this insight, we propose training a neural model to predict the residuals between an $N$-gram model and the actual data distribution. This hybrid approach enables the neural component to concentrate on deeper linguistic understanding while offering a flexible framework for customization; one can switch the underlying $N$-gram model without retraining the neural component. Experiments across three standard tasks—language modeling, machine translation, and summarization—consistently show that our method outperforms existing standalone neural models. Furthermore, the approach facilitates effective domain adaptation by simply swapping in a domain-specific $N$-gram model, requiring no additional training. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ghrua/NgramRes.
This study investigates the performance of Informed OCR (iOCR), a system developed to correct errors in conventional OCR for vote tabulation using a spell correction algorithm. The findings indicate that iOCR outperforms traditional OCR methods. Notably, when processing texts with high error rates from conventional OCR, iOCR reduced error rates by 83.33% and enhanced overall accuracy by 7 points compared to standard approaches. These results demonstrate the superior effectiveness of the informed framework relative to conventional techniques. Furthermore, it is concluded that employing iOCR is far more cost-effective than relying solely on conventional OCR. To access the dataset, visit: https://github.com/monotonically/iOCR-data. The source code for iOCR is available at: https://github.com/monotonically/iOCR.
This study investigates potential global atmospheric circulation patterns in an Earth-like atmosphere using a simplified General Circulation Model (GCM) derived from the University of Hamburg's Portable University Model for the Atmosphere. The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of circulation regimes with respect to planetary rotation closely mirrors findings from laboratory studies on rotating, stratified fluids, particularly when topographic $\beta$-effects are included to simulate planetary vorticity gradients caused by spherical curvature. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate thermal Rossby numbers, with its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber heavily influenced by radiative and frictional damping strengths. These regular waves display notable similarities to baroclinic storms observed on Mars under specific conditions. At the highest rotation rates, multiple jets develop when the Rossby deformation radius and other eddy-related scales are significantly smaller than the planetary radius; these resemble the multiple zonal jets found on gas giant planets. These jets form on scales comparable to the most energetic eddies, poleward of the supercritical latitude, near the Rhines scale. Finally, the balance of heat transport between eddies and zonally symmetric flows varies significantly with rotation rate ($\Omega$), weakening as rotation accelerates. At lower rotation rates, eddies contribute roughly 30% to the total heat flux, but this share drops to nearly zero at the fastest rotation rate examined in this study.
This study presents a real integral formulation for the reciprocal $\Gamma$ function using a regularized hypersingular integral. It confirms the equivalence between this new form and the standard complex representation, subsequently deriving a regularized complex expression that follows the conventional Hankel contour. The work also establishes identities connecting the regularized hypersingular integral, the Hankel contour integral, and a newly introduced contour integral based on a deformed path. These concepts are extended to the regularized complex form defined by the product $\zeta(s)\zeta(s-a)$, replacing the Hankel contour with a similar deformed contour. Additionally, the derivation of these identities implies the regularization of Riemann zeta function products, leading to an identity linking two distinct regularizations of the Riemann zeta function's power. Finally, the regularized hypersingular integral is applied to compute sums of zeta products, including a previously uncalculated identity for the product $\zeta(s)\zeta(s-2)$. Among the key identities derived is an equivalence between the regularized hypersingular integral and the product of zeta functions shifted by an integer, expressed as $\displayline{1/(\Gamma(a)\zeta(a))} = \int_{(a)} (\zeta(s)\zeta(s-a)) (\zeta(s+1)/\zeta(s-1)) \, ds$, which serves as the paper's primary contribution. Among the significant identities derived is the equivalence between the regularized hypersingular integral and the product of zeta functions with an integer shift, given by $\displayline{1/(\Gamma(a)\zeta(a))} = \int_{(a)} (\zeta(s)\zeta(s-a)) (\zeta(s+1)/\zeta(s-1)) \, ds$, which constitutes the principal objective of this work.
Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally challenging. In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, short-wavelength excitation behaviors, and early-time regimes. Based on this framework, we investigate the time-evolution dynamics of spatially inhomogeneous quantum states in systems initially prepared as separated quantum pulses that merge. We present an optimized algorithm significantly reducing the sampling fluctuations typically associated with Monte Carlo methods. These correlations serve as a direct probe for the effective theory, allowing us to determine several transport coefficients, such as viscosities and conductivities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the positive-P method can resolve kinetic theory behaviors, observing the emergence of phonons and turbulent regimes in two-fluid dynamics. Finally, as a generalization of the Wigner-Weyl-Wick formalism, this framework is applicable to a wide range of many-body systems, offering potential extensions beyond interacting Bose gases.

While Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at addressing large-scale problems across numerous domains, their deployment in real-time systems is often hindered by the sheer volume of parameters involved. To overcome this challenge, Teacher-Student architectures were initially introduced in the context of knowledge distillation, enabling lightweight student networks to match the performance of complex teacher models. Recently, these architectures have been widely adopted for diverse knowledge learning tasks, including knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Leveraging such frameworks, recent research has successfully achieved multiple learning objectives through efficient and compact student networks. Unlike previous surveys focused solely on knowledge distillation, this review comprehensively examines Teacher-Student architectures across a spectrum of knowledge learning goals. Furthermore, we systematically outline the processes of knowledge construction and optimization, analyze various architectural designs and learning strategies used to acquire representative and robust knowledge, and summarize recent applications in classification, recognition, and generation. Finally, we explore future research directions concerning architecture design, knowledge quality, and theoretical advancements in regression-based learning. We simulated the ground states of quantum harmonic oscillators subjected to either constant forces of varying magnitudes or time-dependent driving forces. Expectation values of position were computed for different combinations of mass, natural angular frequency, and the coupling constant $\lambda$ under both driving conditions. Under constant forcing, the simulations yielded coherent states. The outcomes for both scenarios align almost perfectly with theoretical predictions. To perform these simulations, we implemented the Metropolis algorithm on a discrete time lattice to evaluate the systems' imaginary time path integrals. Under constant forcing, the path integrals resemble a polynomial well random walk influenced by an external field; under time-dependent forcing, they resemble a simple random walk. Consequently, standard random walk techniques, such as hitting time problems, can be adapted to address these simulations under time-dependent driving. The implemented Metropolis protocol on the discrete lattice is applicable across both constant and time-dependent forcing scenarios. Furthermore, the simulation scheme for constant forcing can potentially be extended to systems under initial momentum excitation, which would correspond to coherent states with non-zero displacement.

Zermelo-Nakano (QHOare) semantics for quantum Hoare logic have been employed to verify that algorithms adhere to linearity—a principle ensuring quantum states are utilized exactly once—by employing before and after linearity bounds within pre and postconditions. This paper introduces a novel reasoning framework termed "expectational relational Hoare logic," which extends QHOare by incorporating expectations into pre- and postconditions. Utilizing this approach, we derive a type system for quantum computation that is linearity-typed up to a factor representing the difference between the anticipated linearity bound and actual linearity. As a demonstration, we apply this type system to a "bind" operation between two quantum programs, which quantifies the leakage of linearity bound due to error correction between the programs. We also outline how to extend this reasoning to prove linearity bounds for more complex compositions of programs, potentially across global and local quantum computation boundaries where error correction is common. Lastly, we sketch how to incorporate reasoning about leakage, which arises when error correction happens outside the scope of quantum reasoning.
This study addresses the bias—defined as over- or underestimation—in the line-of-sight perpendicular component ($B_{\perp}$) of vector magnetic field maps. While prior research has established the existence of this issue, our work conducts novel investigations to quantify the bias, identify its root causes, and propose mitigation strategies. First, we establish quantitative metrics to measure $B_{\perp}$ bias across both local physical components and native image-plane components. Second, we systematically evaluate various inversion methods and data sources, explicitly incorporating the magnetic fill fraction ($ff$), to characterize the impact of these choices. Third, we utilize a simple model to examine how noise and different bias models manifest. Our findings indicate that although the bias predominantly affects under-resolved structures, it also occurs in strong-field pixels that are fully filled. While magnetogram noise can worsen the problem, it is not the primary driver. We demonstrate that explicitly fitting $ff$ offers significant mitigation, though other factors, such as $\chi^2$ weighting and optimization algorithms, also influence results. Furthermore, we present a simple "quick fix" applicable post-facto before resolving the 180° ambiguity in $B_{\perp}$, which is particularly useful when global structures serve as model boundary inputs. These conclusions support the adoption of inversion codes that explicitly fit $ff$ or, as seen with the new SyntHIA neural network, are trained on data derived using this approach. However, we emphasize that this solution relies on the physical plausibility of the actual $ff$; it does not resolve errors introduced by structure-resolving instruments like SyntHIA when they are misconfigured to output integer percentages ranging from 0 to 100 rather than true fractions between 0 and 1. To assist community-wide efforts, we provide open-access formulas (implemented in Python) for estimating $B_{\perp}$ bias under various assumptions, allowing users to assess potential errors in their specific applications. To facilitate this community effort, we have made the complete data set from this study, along with all analysis results, accessible via GitHub (see https://github.com/SyntHIA/Bperp_bias). Additionally, we have developed a set of recommended best practices for vector magnetic field analysis, which will be detailed in an upcoming publication.

Furthermore, we derive straightforward recurrence relations to calculate the number of spheres comprising this wedge. Applicable recurrence relations are also identified for the boolean complex of involutions associated with affine Coxeter groups. Additionally, we derive simple formulas for the Euler characteristics of this complex. Finally, we examine several related complexes, defining two novel complexes and determining their homotopy types. These findings extend recent work by Ragnarsson, Tenner, and the first and second authors concerning these related complexes.

Among the most critical hyperparameters for neural networks, the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. To facilitate this, we have developed a versatile framework applicable to any network architecture or loss option, ensuring fair comparisons. Consequently, we offer a comprehensive benchmark serving as an extensive benchmark suite.
We introduce ATOMIC, a comprehensive atlas of everyday commonsense reasoning structured through 877,000 textual descriptions of inferential knowledge. Unlike existing resources that primarily focus on taxonomic information, ATOMIC emphasizes inferential knowledge formatted as typed if-then relations involving variables (for instance, "if X pays Y a compliment, then Y will likely return the compliment"). To differentiate between causes and effects, agents and themes, voluntary versus involuntary events, and actions versus mental states, we define nine distinct if-then relation types. By generatively training neural models on the rich inferential knowledge within ATOMIC, we demonstrate that these models can acquire basic commonsense abilities and reason about unseen events. Furthermore, experimental findings indicate that multitask models utilizing the hierarchical structure of these if-then relation types achieve more accurate inference than those trained in isolation, a result confirmed by both automated metrics and human evaluation. To facilitate access to this commonsense resources, we provide an API available at www.atomic-commonsense.com.

A graph $G=(V,E)$ equipped with geodesic distance $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ is considered resolved by a non-empty vertex subset $R$ if, for every pair of vertices $u$ and $v$, the condition $d(u,r)=d(v,r)$ holding for all $r\in R$ implies $u=v$. The metric dimension of $G$ corresponds to the size of its minimal resolving set. This manuscript introduces and examines the concepts of resolvability and metric dimension under a truncated geodesic distance defined by a threshold $k$, utilizing the metric $d_k(u,v):=\min\{d(u,v),k+1\}$. We define the metric dimension of $G$ relative to $d_k$ as $\beta_k(G)$. The study analyzes how $\beta_k(G)$ varies with respect to $k$ and the graph's diameter. Furthermore, we characterize the truncated metric dimension for paths, cycles, and graphs exhibiting extreme dimensions, specifically those of order $n$ where $\beta_k(G)=n-2$ or $\beta_k(G)=n-1$. The work concludes with an exploration of several issues concerning the truncated metric dimension of trees. To facilitate these investigations, we define several characteristics and operations on graphs that facilitate proofs regarding the truncated metric dimension. Additionally, we establish relationships between the truncated metric dimension and other graphical parameters, while identifying the truncated geodesic balls that constitute minimal resolving sets. Finally, we characterize groups of graphs that possess a specific truncated metric dimension. These findings extend previous research on metric dimension to the context of the truncated distance, resulting in a series of notable theorems and lemmas highlighted within this manuscript. These insights may find applications in chemistry, biology, and information theory, particularly in damage localization, as discussed in these notes. To underscore the relevance of studied graph examples, we provide a characterization of the truncated metric dimension for various standard graph families. Furthermore, we propose several problems and define additional properties aimed at advancing future research in this area.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies with measured total luminosities for the two fine-structure transitions of neutral atomic carbon ($^{3}P_1 \rightarrow ^{3}P_{0}$ and $^{3}P_2 \rightarrow ^{3}P_{1}$), determining that their average excitation conditions are strongly subthermal. This conclusion was drawn from modeling the CI(2-1)/(1-0) ratios ($R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$) using exact solutions for a 3-level system, without relying on specific assumptions regarding the kinematic state of the associated $\rm H_2$ gas or its line formation mechanism. This non-LTE excitation likely explains the recent findings by Valentino et al. (2020) regarding a curious clustering of gas temperatures near $\sim$25 K when derived under LTE assumptions—a clustering that shows no correlation with actual gas temperatures. Consequently, non-LTE excitation in the interstellar medium complicates simple estimates of molecular gas temperatures and introduces uncertainty into CI-based mass calculations, particularly when utilizing the J=2-1 line. Nevertheless, the $R^{(ci)}_{21/10} = \rm F(n, T_{k})$ ratio offers significant value for combined CO/CI spectral energy distribution (SLED) and dust spectral energy distribution (SED) models, remaining independent of assumptions inherent in CO radiative transfer models, such as the LVG approximation. Finally, we hypothesize that the coexistence of low $R^{(ci)}_{21/10}$ ratios ($\leq 1$) and high dust temperatures ($\rm T_{dust}$) in certain extreme starbursts signals the presence of massive, low-density molecular winds and/or circumgalactic gas reservoirs. If confirmed through imaging observations, this metric could serve as a useful indicator for identifying such reservoirs in galaxies.
We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions and a second-class particle originating at zero, the particle's velocity converges almost surely to a uniform distribution on $[-1,1]$ as time approaches infinity. This result affirmatively settles Conjectures 1.9 and 1.10 from [Amir, Angel and Valko, "The TASEP speed process", Annals of Probability 39, 1205--1242, 2011] and enables the construction of the ASEP speed process. Furthermore, we establish that ASEP coupled via the multi-particle system process possesses a unique ergodic stationary distribution, provided the jump rates satisfy certain conditions. Finally, utilizing the speed process, we show that ASEP coupled through the current process also converges to uniqueness upon imposing an additional irreversibility condition on the jump rates. Lastly, we utilize the hydrodynamic limit to derive the equilibrium distribution of the current process under this same irreversibility constraint.

Advancements in technology have enabled big data processing, yet this has created substantial computational challenges when solving large-scale linear systems or performing matrix inversions. Consequently, there has been significant research into fast, approximate iterative methods for matrix inversion accelerated by Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), offering viable alternatives where traditional direct inversion methods are too costly. Existing techniques include the Neumann Series (NS), Newton iteration (NI), Chebyshev Iteration (CI), and Successive Over-Relaxation. This study introduces a novel iterative algorithm derived from the NS, termed "Nested Neumann" (NN). This approach generalizes higher-order iterations of NI and CI by leveraging a computationally efficient iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, dependent on a specified "inception depth." Mathematical analysis confirms that the NN method: (i) converges provided the preconditioning matrix satisfies the spectral norm condition required for NS, (ii) achieves a convergence rate equivalent to an order of (inception depth plus one), and (iii) performs optimally with an inception depth of one or two, contingent upon available RAM. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for NN suitable for massive sparse matrices, accounting for increased computational costs. Crucially, we establish an analytical equivalence between NS and NN (including NI, CI, and higher orders), a finding particularly relevant for mMIMO systems. Finally, the NN method is applicable to positive semi-definite matrices for inversion and can be utilized for any linear system, whether sparse, non-sparse, or complex. Contextual linear bandits represent a theoretically significant model with extensive practical utility, recently attracting considerable attention in wireless applications where communication constraints often limit performance, particularly when contexts exist in a high-dimensional $d$-dimensional space. This paper addresses a distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit learning scenario where agents observe contexts and select actions, yet are geographically separated from the central learner who performs the optimization without direct access to the contexts. Assuming contexts follow a specific distribution, we introduce a method requiring approximately $5d$ bits per context when the distribution is unknown, and zero bits per context if it is known. This approach achieves a regret bound nearly identical to that of a fully observable setting. Specifically, the bound for the unknown distribution case improves upon existing results by a $\log(T)$ factor (where $T$ is the time horizon), while the bound for the known distribution case reaches information-theoretic tightness. Numerical experiments using a stochastic linear bandit problem demonstrate that the proposed algorithm effectively replaces the $T$ contexts needed for traditional distributed learning with merely $5d$ bits per context. Furthermore, these experiments confirm that the actual performance regret remains close to the theoretical regret bound even in early stages of learning. Leveraging the new algorithmic framework, we also derive a nearly tight regret upper bound for the k-th best arm problem across distributed memoryless contextual bandits. The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism dependent on rapid gas cooling, potentially active in the outer zones of protoplanetary disks. While the VSI generates turbulence characterized by vigorous vertical motions that can influence dust accumulation and settling, dust evolution itself can suppress this instability. Specifically, as dust grows and settles, it depletes the gas, rendering cooling inefficient in the optically thin outer regions. This study employs linear analysis to quantify how dust evolution stabilizes the VSI. We developed a cooling timescale model incorporating dust growth beyond micron scales and size-dependent settling. By integrating this model with linear stability analysis, we identified the "VSI zone" and calculated the maximum growth rate at various radial distances. Our results indicate that both dust growth and settling restrict the VSI zone to the immediate vicinity of the midplane. Consequently, the instability's growth rate diminishes because the vertical shear of rotational velocity—the instability's driving force—is weaker at lower altitudes. In our default model of a 0.01 solar mass disk, dust growth from 10 microns to 1 mm reduces the growth rate by a factor exceeding 10. Ultimately, the suppression of VSI-driven turbulence by dust evolution could accelerate further dust processing in outer disk regions and account for the significant dust settling observed in the HL Tau system. This paper presents an enhanced model integrating dust growth, settling, and the VSI, available at https://github.com/joergensohn/VSIDust.

The rise of outsourced training and machine learning as a service has introduced new attack vectors, specifically backdoor attacks. These attacks conceal a secret function within a neural network that activates only when a specific trigger is present in the input. While most existing literature assumes static triggers with fixed locations and patterns—properties upon which many detection mechanisms rely—recent studies have demonstrated that image classification countermeasures like Neural Cleanse and ABS can be circumvented using dynamic triggers that remain effective regardless of their position or appearance. However, such dynamic backdoors are resource-intensive, typically requiring a significant portion of poisoned training data. This work presents the first demonstration that dynamic backdoor attacks can occur via a global average pooling layer without needing an increased volume of poisoned data. Despite this theoretical possibility, experimental results across sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification indicate that implementing such attacks remains highly challenging in practice. These findings underscore the importance of validating assumptions behind potential attacks before investing resources to neutralize them. To facilitate this verification, we released a set of tools designed to detect backdoor attacks, which are available at https://github.com/willyouneverguess/SDS.
This work addresses the challenge of a Parameter Server (PS) learning a model from data distributed across graph nodes, with Federated Learning (FL) serving as the primary application. A significant hurdle in FL is the communication bottleneck between nodes and the PS. Although performing multiple local updates per iteration before syncing with the PS is a common strategy to alleviate this bottleneck, the statistical heterogeneity of node-specific data often results in biased models and delayed convergence. To overcome both communication and data heterogeneity issues, we investigate Random Walk (RW) learning algorithms. These algorithms utilize direct connections between nodes, which are typically more efficient than communicating with the PS. In this framework, the model acts as a "baton" passed iteratively to a neighboring node after each update. Designing effective RW algorithms is complicated by data heterogeneity and uncertainty regarding data distributions; ideally, nodes with more informative data should be visited more frequently. We formulate this as a sleeping multi-armed bandit (MAB) problem to develop a near-optimal node sampling strategy that minimizes gradient estimate variance and asymptotically approaches optimal sampling. Building on this, we propose an adaptive random walk learning algorithm and provide theoretical convergence guarantees. Our numerical experiments confirm these theoretical results and demonstrate that our algorithm surpasses existing random walk methods. Furthermore, we conduct an end-to-end FL experiment using image classification on the CIFAR-10 dataset, showing that our proposed algorithm overcomes communication bottlenecks between nodes and the PS.

Decisions regarding the rejection of null hypotheses ($H_0$) in cognitive science rely heavily on the strength of evidence supporting alternative hypotheses ($H_1$). We present an implementation of a deep learning framework designed to explore dark matter structure formation. Specifically, we examine how velocity and density field data influence the construction of the halo mass function using cosmological $N$-body simulations. Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass into which individual particles will collapse by $z=0$, within the range $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. Our findings indicate that incorporating velocity alongside density information yields negligible improvements when utilizing simulations based on the standard $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model with an initial scalar perturbation amplitude of $A_s = 2\times10^{-9}$. To analyze ellipsoidal collapse models and assess velocity effects in smaller mass regimes, we increased the initial power spectrum. This adjustment allowed us to observe velocity impacts on larger halos that fall within our simulation's resolution. Consequently, the CNN model trained on simulations with a higher $A_s$ demonstrated significant improvements in halo mass prediction when velocity field data were included. Ultimately, for simulations where $A_s = 8 \times 10^{-8}$, the model relying solely on density information exhibited at least an $80\%$ increase in mean squared error compared to the model utilizing both velocity and density across nearly all mass scales, highlighting the failure of the density-only approach in this scenario. Our results conclude that the influence of the velocity field on halo collapse is scale-dependent, exerting a negligible effect under the standard cosmological model for mass scales between $10.5 < \log(M/ M_{\odot}) < 14$. To facilitate future investigations into structure formation, we make the simulation outputs and source code accessible at https://github.com/Nirmalya/HaloNeuralNet.
Detecting magnetic fields with high sensitivity remains a significant challenge in metrology. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. Although the direct detection of the Meissner effect has already been achieved with much lower precision, this approach could enable experiments with even higher sensitivity. Such capabilities might facilitate the investigation of the magnetic monopole image force exerted on a superconductor and tests of the Kramers relation among critical phenomena, which predicts the existence of an analogous image field in materials exhibiting superfluidity. As a result, this technique could find applications in quantum metrology, helping to define the SI unit of magnetic field intensity, and in characterizing the transition state where the magnetic field is expelled from a superconductor or a material transitioning into superfluidity. Furthermore, this method could serve as a means to search for magnetic monopoles.
We introduce a fully relativistic, first-principles theoretical framework designed to calculate the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities situated on superconducting surfaces, thereby establishing a material-specific methodology for analyzing Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states. Through a detailed orbital decomposition of local densities of states, we examine the formation mechanisms of YSR states for an Mn adatom and two configurations of Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface, contrasting our theoretical outcomes with recent experimental data. For the adatom, our findings indicate that spin-orbit coupling causes minor shifts in certain YSR peaks, while local spin-polarization on Nb atoms has negligible influence on their positions. Furthermore, scaling the exchange field at the Mn site accounts for the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum. Our results for a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer align well with the experimentally observed splitting of YSR states; however, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, the spin-orbit coupling proves insufficient to explain the experimentally observed splitting. Additionally, altering the relative orientation of magnetic moments within this dimer induces splitting and energy shifts of the YSR states, ultimately resulting in the emergence of a zero-bias peak for the deepest YSR state.
This report outlines the methodologies that secured 3rd and 4th place in tasks 1 and 2, respectively, at the ISIC 2019 challenge, which aims to diagnose skin cancer using images and metadata. Although the dataset contains nine classes, one is an outlier and absent from the actual data. To address this, we employed an ensemble of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNNs), developed two strategies to manage the missing outlier class, and introduced a simple technique for integrating metadata with image data. We detail each methodology and its parameters throughout this document to ensure replicability. Our results align with previous challenges, and our approaches for detecting the outlier class and leveraging metadata have proven effective. Future challenges should focus on improving the classification of this rarely observed outlier class. Our methods and initial tests will participate in the ISIC 2020 challenge, and we have already adapted our methodology to process the 2020 dataset for an upcoming challenge. This work will also be applied to the Melanoma 200 Dataset, a smaller collection of 2000 images from the challenge's earlier iterations. Findings from this study could benefit the medical community and help advance early melanoma detection. Focusing on muon colliders, we re-examine the validity of $W$ and $Z$ parton distribution functions (PDFs) at leading order for $2\to n$ processes. These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. By synthesizing these approaches, we derive an "incompleteness theorem" applicable to a broader class of formal systems than those covered by Godel's original theorem. Subsequently, we adapt the method used by Tarski, Godel, and Carnap to establish their undefinability results. Although efforts have been made to create analogous "incompleteness" results for specific non-standard formal systems—such as those by Smullyan (1978), Hyland and MacIntosh (1981), and Mountjoy (2015)—there remains a demand for further investigation into these systems to develop corresponding undefinability theorems. Consequently, this paper concludes with an invitation to explore how to adapt the techniques from Godel's first incompleteness theorem and Tarski's undefinability theorem to establish an undefinability result for a particular non-standard formal system introduced by Kripke (1942).

Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. Finally, we summarize approaches for verifying the invariance of arbitrary sets in systems governed by non-linear non-integral operators.

This study examines the coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino behavior, and dark matter properties within the minimal scoto-seesaw framework. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. We pinpoint parameter regions that satisfy theoretical constraints, align with dark matter relic density, and are viable under direct detection limits. Employing two-loop renormalization group equations, we investigate vacuum stability and the consistency of the fundamental dark parity symmetry, while also deriving a lower bound for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Furthermore, we produce a comprehensive phenomenological map highlighting potentials for observation at current and upcoming direct dark matter searches, as well as neutrinoless double beta decay experiments.
